entries.newText: The workshop combines machinery with specific rights to choose tasks and stop unsafe work. Community ownership alone would not guarantee those powers.

entries.originalDescription: The older account of worthwhile making shapes an institutional proposal without promising that all necessary labour becomes delightful.

originalReading.text: The older account of worthwhile making shapes an institutional proposal without promising that all necessary labour becomes delightful.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase or teaching reconstruction; not a quotation. entries.newText: The workshop values skill and the maker's experience as well as output. Its design does not promise that every necessary task becomes enjoyable.

entries.originalDescription: An unresolved practical obligation remains inside the proposed good life.

originalReading.text: An unresolved practical obligation remains inside the proposed good life.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase or teaching reconstruction; not a quotation. entries.newText: Pleasurable making leaves care and maintenance to be done. A good-life proposal must still decide how that work is supported and shared.

originalReading.text: A bounded autonomous arrangement is adapted from an observatory to a social setting with much more contested consequences.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase or teaching reconstruction; not a quotation. Sources: Authored speculative constructions; background: Ostrom Nobel lecture; Ostrom, Beyond Markets and States (2009), Nobel Prize lecture, pp.417, 419, 422, 429; William Morris Archive: Useful Work versus Useless Toil; Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution; NIST AI RMF Core

entries.newText: The imagined city uses local signals to respond to urgent problems. Unlike a remote observatory, its choices directly involve conflicting human priorities.

entries.originalDescription: The conflict is kept explicit: responsiveness and prior contestability can pull in different directions.

originalReading.text: The conflict is kept explicit: responsiveness and prior contestability can pull in different directions.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase or teaching reconstruction; not a quotation. Sources: Authored speculative constructions; background: Ostrom Nobel lecture; Ostrom, Beyond Markets and States (2009), Nobel Prize lecture, pp.417, 419, 422, 429; William Morris Archive: Useful Work versus Useless Toil; Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution; NIST AI RMF Core

entries.newText: Faster action leaves less time to object before it happens. The design must face that conflict instead of promising both benefits without cost.

entries.originalDescription: Appeal supplies a partial institutional response, not a cure for damage already done or time already lost.

originalReading.text: Appeal supplies a partial institutional response, not a cure for damage already done or time already lost.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase or teaching reconstruction; not a quotation. Sources: Authored speculative constructions; background: Ostrom Nobel lecture; Ostrom, Beyond Markets and States (2009), Nobel Prize lecture, pp.417, 419, 422, 429; William Morris Archive: Useful Work versus Useless Toil; Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution; NIST AI RMF Core

entries.newText: Residents can examine and appeal rapid decisions. This adds accountability but cannot undo every harm or recover lost time.

entries.originalDescription: Modern-to-future comparison: the possibility of cooperation does not itself design an institution; rulemaking does additional work.

originalReading.text: Modern-to-future comparison: the possibility of cooperation does not itself design an institution; rulemaking does additional work.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase or teaching reconstruction; not a quotation. Sources: Authored speculative constructions; background: Ostrom Nobel lecture; Ostrom, Beyond Markets and States (2009), Nobel Prize lecture, pp.417, 419, 422, 429; William Morris Archive: Useful Work versus Useless Toil; Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution; NIST AI RMF Core

entries.newText: Cooperation is supported by rules that affected people can change. Willingness to cooperate alone does not design a workable institution.

entries.originalDescription: The older distinction between aggregate wealth and living well remains useful in judging what the new production system is for.

originalReading.text: The older distinction between aggregate wealth and living well remains useful in judging what the new production system is for.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase or teaching reconstruction; not a quotation. entries.newText: A prosperous city need not require everyone to pursue the same life. Wealth is one consideration, not a complete definition of living well.

entries.originalDescription: The ending preserves an institutional proposal and an unresolved burden. It does not synthesize every disagreement into a universal solution.

originalReading.text: The ending preserves an institutional proposal and an unresolved burden. It does not synthesize every disagreement into a universal solution.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase or teaching reconstruction; not a quotation. Sources: Authored speculative constructions; background: Ostrom Nobel lecture; Ostrom, Beyond Markets and States (2009), Nobel Prize lecture, pp.417, 419, 422, 429; William Morris Archive: Useful Work versus Useless Toil; Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution; NIST AI RMF Core

entries.newText: The proposed society still has disagreements and responsibilities, especially care and fair control of decisions. The story ends with work remaining, not one solution to every problem.

entries.originalDescription: Aristotle asks what political association is for, not only how it prevents injury.

originalReading.text: Aristotle asks what political association is for, not only how it prevents injury.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Aristotle, Politics III.1, III.6–9

entries.newText: For Aristotle, a city supports a shared way of life through courts and public offices. Its purpose is more than preventing people from injuring one another.

entries.originalDescription: Aristotle distinguishes common advantage from the rulers’ advantage.

originalReading.text: Aristotle distinguishes common advantage from the rulers’ advantage.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Aristotle, Politics III.1, III.6–9

entries.newText: One person, a few people or many people may rule for their own advantage. Aristotle asks whose interests the government serves.

entries.originalDescription: A definition of political participation, not a claim that all inhabitants possessed it.

originalReading.text: A definition of political participation, not a claim that all inhabitants possessed it.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Aristotle, Politics III.1, III.6–9

entries.newText: Aristotle defines citizenship through participation in judgment and office. This did not include every person living in the city.

entries.originalDescription: The city depends on people excluded from its citizen assembly. Status and institutions varied across poleis.

originalReading.text: The city depends on people excluded from its citizen assembly. Status and institutions varied across poleis.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Aristotle, Politics III.1, III.6–9

entries.newText: Women, enslaved people and resident foreigners were excluded from Athens's citizen assembly. Other Greek cities had different arrangements, but ancient citizenship was not universal.

entries.originalDescription: The ship analogy puts knowledge beside the struggle to command.

originalReading.text: The ship analogy puts knowledge beside the struggle to command.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Plato, Republic VI, ship analogy (488a–489a)

entries.newText: In Plato's ship comparison, sailors fight for command while ignoring the person who knows how to navigate. The example links ruling with knowledge rather than popularity.

entries.originalDescription: Teaching comparison: practical judgment now asks what a political community makes possible.

originalReading.text: Teaching comparison: practical judgment now asks what a political community makes possible.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Aristotle, Politics III.1, III.6–9

entries.newText: Political life can be judged by what it enables people to share and achieve. Asking about a common good also raises the question of who is included.

entries.originalDescription: A constitutional classification tests purposes as well as numbers.

originalReading.text: A constitutional classification tests purposes as well as numbers.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Aristotle, Politics III.1, III.6–9

entries.newText: A government is judged by whose interests it serves, not only by how many people rule. A ruler's benefit can differ from the community's.

entries.originalDescription: A boundary of ancient citizenship remains visible rather than becoming modern equality.

originalReading.text: A boundary of ancient citizenship remains visible rather than becoming modern equality.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Aristotle, Politics III.1, III.6–9

entries.newText: Living in a city does not necessarily give a person a political voice. Ancient citizenship excluded many people on whom the city depended.

entries.originalDescription: A modern critical question about the ancient argument; not an egalitarian conclusion attributed to Aristotle.

originalReading.text: A modern critical question about the ancient argument; not an egalitarian conclusion attributed to Aristotle.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Aristotle, Politics III.1, III.6–9

entries.newText: A city can claim to serve a common good while denying many inhabitants a political voice. Whose good is included, and whose interests are left out?

entries.originalDescription: Plato links rule with knowledge of what is good. His ship analogy remains beside, not a resolution of, the citizenship question.

originalReading.text: Plato links rule with knowledge of what is good. His ship analogy remains beside, not a resolution of, the citizenship question.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Plato, Republic VI, ship analogy (488a–489a)

entries.newText: Plato argues that ruling requires knowledge of what is good, not simply winning support. The claim does not settle who should be allowed a political voice.

entries.originalDescription: These statuses are not interchangeable with citizenship, political participation or modern legal personhood.

originalReading.text: These statuses are not interchangeable with citizenship, political participation or modern legal personhood.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem

entries.newText: Roman law distinguishes freeborn, freed and enslaved people. Those legal statuses are not the same as citizenship or participation in government.

entries.originalDescription: The compilation nevertheless regulates slavery; the statement does not abolish it.

originalReading.text: The compilation nevertheless regulates slavery; the statement does not abolish it.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem

entries.newText: Justinian's Institutes describe slavery as contrary to nature while also regulating it. The statement does not abolish the institution.

entries.originalDescription: Manumission changes an individual’s status inside the legal system.

originalReading.text: Manumission changes an individual’s status inside the legal system.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem

entries.newText: Manumission legally frees an individual enslaved person. It changes that person's status within a system that still permits slavery.

entries.originalDescription: Sixth-century imperial compilation is not neutral preservation of every older disagreement.

originalReading.text: Sixth-century imperial compilation is not neutral preservation of every older disagreement.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem

entries.newText: Justinian orders older law selected and edited into an authoritative collection. The result decides what has legal force rather than preserving every disagreement neutrally.

entries.originalDescription: Teaching comparison of Greek participation with Roman statuses; no identity between the systems is implied.

originalReading.text: Teaching comparison of Greek participation with Roman statuses; no identity between the systems is implied.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem

entries.newText: Roman law divides people by legal status in ways different from Greek political participation. Comparing the two systems does not make them identical.

entries.originalDescription: Both legal statements remain on the desk; no philosophical victory automatically changes the institution.

originalReading.text: Both legal statements remain on the desk; no philosophical victory automatically changes the institution.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem

entries.newText: The law calls slavery contrary to nature and still upholds it. A stated principle can conflict with the institution that enforces it.

entries.originalDescription: This legal transition is not universal emancipation.

originalReading.text: This legal transition is not universal emancipation.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem

entries.newText: An enslaved person becomes legally freed. This individual change is not the abolition of slavery for everyone.

entries.originalDescription: A distinction between a remedy within slavery and ending slavery as an institution.

originalReading.text: A distinction between a remedy within slavery and ending slavery as an institution.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem

entries.newText: A route for freeing individuals leaves slavery as an institution in place. Relief within a system differs from ending the system.

entries.originalDescription: Teaching contrast: a critical edition exposes variants; an authorized compilation also selects what has legal force.

originalReading.text: Teaching contrast: a critical edition exposes variants; an authorized compilation also selects what has legal force.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem

entries.newText: The emperor's collection selects which older law is authoritative. Unlike an edition that displays variants, it also determines which text has legal force.

entries.originalDescription: Medieval copies visibly surround inherited law with interpretation.

originalReading.text: Medieval copies visibly surround inherited law with interpretation.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. UC Berkeley, The Medieval Law School: manuscripts of Justinian with glosses

entries.newText: Medieval readers at Bologna write explanations around and between the lines of Justinian's law. The inherited text becomes surrounded by new interpretation.

entries.originalDescription: Reception at Bologna is documented; its medieval application is not the unchanged continuation of a sixth-century empire.

originalReading.text: Reception at Bologna is documented; its medieval application is not the unchanged continuation of a sixth-century empire.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. UC Berkeley, The Medieval Law School: manuscripts of Justinian with glosses

entries.newText: Medieval commentary gives Roman law new uses and meanings. It is documented reception, not the unchanged continuation of Justinian's empire.

entries.originalDescription: The argument responds to insecurity, not a historical claim that humans once signed a universal pact.

originalReading.text: The argument responds to insecurity, not a historical claim that humans once signed a universal pact.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan XVII–XVIII and XXI (1651)

entries.newText: Hobbes argues that rival private powers cannot reliably secure peace. He uses an agreement to authorize common power as an explanation of political authority.

entries.originalDescription: Hobbes makes subjects covenant with one another. The sovereign is not a contracting subject.

originalReading.text: Hobbes makes subjects covenant with one another. The sovereign is not a contracting subject.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan XVII–XVIII and XXI (1651)

entries.newText: In Hobbes's account, people agree with one another to authorize a ruler or assembly. The sovereign is not simply another party bound by the same agreement.

entries.originalDescription: Hobbes ties obligation to the power to protect; not every disliked decision voids authority.

originalReading.text: Hobbes ties obligation to the power to protect; not every disliked decision voids authority.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan XVII–XVIII and XXI (1651)

entries.newText: Hobbes connects obedience with the sovereign's power to protect. Losing protection matters differently from merely disliking a decision.

entries.originalDescription: Consent can authorize majority decisions. Locke’s account and its practical reach remain contestable.

originalReading.text: Consent can authorize majority decisions. Locke’s account and its practical reach remain contestable.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. John Locke, Second Treatise §§95–99, 119–122, 221–222 (1689/90)

entries.newText: Locke argues that legitimate political society requires consent. That can authorize majority decisions, while the account's practical reach remains open to criticism.

entries.originalDescription: Locke treats this as a breach of the trust for which government was established.

originalReading.text: Locke treats this as a breach of the trust for which government was established.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. John Locke, Second Treatise §§95–99, 119–122, 221–222 (1689/90)

entries.newText: Rulers act arbitrarily against lives, liberties or possessions. Locke treats this as violating the trust for which government was established.

entries.originalDescription: Teaching comparison: the ancient question of political benefit receives a distinct early modern answer.

originalReading.text: Teaching comparison: the ancient question of political benefit receives a distinct early modern answer.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan XVII–XVIII and XXI (1651)

entries.newText: Hobbes makes protection a central purpose of political authority. This answers the question of political benefit differently from the ancient accounts.

entries.originalDescription: Reconstruction of a political argument, not proof that undivided power always brings peace.

originalReading.text: Reconstruction of a political argument, not proof that undivided power always brings peace.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan XVII–XVIII and XXI (1651)

entries.newText: Hobbes argues that authorized sovereign power can secure peace. The argument does not prove that concentrated power always succeeds.

entries.originalDescription: The argument preserves a limit grounded in self-preservation.

originalReading.text: The argument preserves a limit grounded in self-preservation.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan XVII–XVIII and XXI (1651)

entries.newText: For Hobbes, a subject's obligation can end when the sovereign can no longer protect them. Self-preservation places a limit on obedience.

entries.originalDescription: Teaching comparison: shared humanity and legitimate political membership are different claims; no direct Stoic derivation is asserted.

originalReading.text: Teaching comparison: shared humanity and legitimate political membership are different claims; no direct Stoic derivation is asserted.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. John Locke, Second Treatise §§95–99, 119–122, 221–222 (1689/90)

entries.newText: Locke grounds legitimate government in consent. Sharing humanity is not itself the same as consenting to a particular political authority.

entries.originalDescription: A right argued for, not a guarantee that resistance succeeds or that everyone was enfranchised.

originalReading.text: A right argued for, not a guarantee that resistance succeeds or that everyone was enfranchised.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. John Locke, Second Treatise §§95–99, 119–122, 221–222 (1689/90)

entries.newText: Locke argues that a government's breach of trust can justify resistance. This does not guarantee success or imply that everyone then had an equal vote.

entries.originalDescription: The accounts remain distinct; social contract is not a single settled doctrine.

originalReading.text: The accounts remain distinct; social contract is not a single settled doctrine.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan XVII–XVIII and XXI (1651); John Locke, Second Treatise §§95–99, 119–122, 221–222 (1689/90)

entries.newText: Hobbes and Locke give different accounts of protection, consent and resistance. Social-contract thinking is not one settled doctrine.

entries.originalDescription: Political agency changes the situation; emancipation is not simply an idea exported from a European desk.

originalReading.text: Political agency changes the situation; emancipation is not simply an idea exported from a European desk.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Mémorial de l’abolition de l’esclavage, chronology of abolition; Library of Congress / Bibliothèque Haïtienne des Pères du Saint-Esprit: Laws of Saint-Domingue (1801)

entries.newText: In 1791, enslaved people rise against plantation slavery in Saint-Domingue. Their action changes the political situation; emancipation is not merely an idea sent from Europe.

entries.originalDescription: Abolition followed uprising, conflict and political pressure; this card is not a claim of uniform immediate enforcement.

originalReading.text: Abolition followed uprising, conflict and political pressure; this card is not a claim of uniform immediate enforcement.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Mémorial de l’abolition de l’esclavage, chronology of abolition; BnF, Haiti’s independence debt: archival context, 1794–1922

entries.newText: Decrees in 1793–1794 abolish slavery amid uprising, war and political pressure. A legal change does not mean immediate, uniform enforcement.

entries.originalDescription: The constitution rejects slavery while retaining the colonial connection.

originalReading.text: The constitution rejects slavery while retaining the colonial connection.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Constitution of Saint-Domingue, 1801, arts.1–5, 14–16, 28

entries.newText: The 1801 constitution rejects slavery while keeping Saint-Domingue connected to France. Abolition and independence are not yet the same achievement.

entries.originalDescription: The same constitution maintains a compulsory agricultural order. Ending slavery does not mean free choice of work.

originalReading.text: The same constitution maintains a compulsory agricultural order. Ending slavery does not mean free choice of work.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Constitution of Saint-Domingue, 1801, arts.1–5, 14–16, 28

entries.newText: The 1801 constitution keeps a compulsory plantation system. Ending slavery does not automatically give workers freedom to choose their work.

entries.originalDescription: Separation was fought for, not inferred from a declaration of rights. The declaration does not establish equal power for all.

originalReading.text: Separation was fought for, not inferred from a declaration of rights. The declaration does not establish equal power for all.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Haitian Declaration of Independence (1804), Dubois/Garrigus translation; BnF, Haiti’s independence debt: archival context, 1794–1922

entries.newText: After defeating French reconquest, Haiti declares independence in 1804. Independence was fought for and did not immediately create equal power for everyone.

entries.originalDescription: The earlier liberty claim meets the agency of enslaved people, not passive receipt of Enlightenment ideas.

originalReading.text: The earlier liberty claim meets the agency of enslaved people, not passive receipt of Enlightenment ideas.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. BnF, Haiti’s independence debt: archival context, 1794–1922

entries.newText: Enslaved insurgents make freedom an active political demand. They are agents of change, not passive recipients of European ideas.

entries.originalDescription: A changed legal status is distinguished from both an abstract promise and its enforcement.

originalReading.text: A changed legal status is distinguished from both an abstract promise and its enforcement.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. BnF, Haiti’s independence debt: archival context, 1794–1922

entries.newText: Emancipation becomes law during the revolution. Legal status changes, while enforcement and freedom in daily life remain further questions.

entries.originalDescription: The 1801 text keeps two propositions that later events will pull apart.

originalReading.text: The 1801 text keeps two propositions that later events will pull apart.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Constitution of Saint-Domingue, 1801, arts.1–5, 14–16, 28

entries.newText: The 1801 constitution combines abolition with continued membership in the French empire. Those two claims need to be distinguished.

entries.originalDescription: Teaching comparison: a political ideal tests work arrangements; no direct Locke-to-Louverture influence is claimed.

originalReading.text: Teaching comparison: a political ideal tests work arrangements; no direct Locke-to-Louverture influence is claimed.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. John Locke, Second Treatise §§95–99, 119–122, 221–222 (1689/90); Constitution of Saint-Domingue, 1801, arts.1–5, 14–16, 28

entries.newText: Compulsory plantation work prevents people from freely choosing their work. It puts the ideal of consent in conflict with the actual working arrangement.

entries.originalDescription: An institutional contradiction survives; the game does not undo the achievement of emancipation.

originalReading.text: An institutional contradiction survives; the game does not undo the achievement of emancipation.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Constitution of Saint-Domingue, 1801, arts.1–5, 14–16, 28

entries.newText: Abolition coexists with compulsory labour. Recognizing that conflict does not erase the achievement of ending slavery.

entries.originalDescription: Independence breaks France’s claim to rule, not every coercive social relation. International recognition was not automatic.

originalReading.text: Independence breaks France’s claim to rule, not every coercive social relation. International recognition was not automatic.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Haitian Declaration of Independence (1804), Dubois/Garrigus translation; BnF, Haiti’s independence debt: archival context, 1794–1922

entries.newText: Haiti's independence breaks France's claim to rule and defends emancipation. It does not remove every form of coercion or secure immediate international recognition.

entries.originalDescription: Speculative return: formal emancipation alone did not secure freedom at work; the proposed institution needs contestable rules, not a triumphant rights label.

originalReading.text: Speculative return: formal emancipation alone did not secure freedom at work; the proposed institution needs contestable rules, not a triumphant rights label.
originalReading.attribution: Authored paraphrase / teaching reconstruction, not a quotation. Authored speculative constructions; background: Ostrom Nobel lecture; Constitution of Saint-Domingue, 1801, arts.1–5, 14–16, 28; Ostrom, Beyond Markets and States (2009), Nobel Prize lecture, pp.417, 419, 422, 429

entries.newText: The imagined shared-resource institution must let people challenge coercive rules. A formal promise of freedom is not enough to guarantee freedom in work.

entries.originalDescription: Loose ground: mineral grit, clay and the material in which roots grow.
entries.newText: Loose ground containing mineral grains and clay. Plants can grow in suitable soil.

entries.originalDescription: Flowing, soaking and carrying; a liquid that takes the shape of its container.
entries.newText: A liquid that flows, soaks materials and takes the shape of its container.

entries.originalDescription: The invisible moving world around us. It carries moisture and feeds a flame.
entries.newText: The gases around us. Moving air can carry moisture, fill a sail and supply oxygen to a flame.

entries.originalDescription: Heat and light. It cooks, hardens and changes materials rather than merely joining them.
entries.newText: Burning produces heat and light. Heat can cook food and change materials.

entries.originalDescription: A shaped, dried but unfired clay bowl. It is a dry forming surface, not a water-ready vessel.
entries.newText: A shaped, dried clay bowl that has not been fired. It can serve as a dry form, but is not ready to hold water.

entries.originalDescription: Loose strands from plant stems. Flexible, but not yet organized into a strong length or sheet.
entries.newText: Flexible strands taken from plants. They can be spun into thread or made into sheets.

entries.originalDescription: Thicker cordage that can hold a load or keep larger pieces together.
entries.newText: Thick cord made to hold loads or tie larger pieces together.

entries.originalDescription: Wheels mounted on a wooden axle: a rolling undercarriage, not yet a load-carrying body.
entries.newText: Wheels mounted on an axle. They can roll, but still need a body to carry a load.

entries.originalDescription: A wooden wheel with teeth cut around its rim, able to pass rotation to another mechanism.
entries.newText: A wooden wheel with teeth that transfer turning motion to another part.

entries.originalDescription: A living flour culture. Given moisture and time, it makes gas and changes dough.
entries.newText: A culture of microorganisms in flour and water. Given time, it produces gas that helps dough rise.

entries.originalDescription: Dough expanded by fermentation, with small bubbles held inside it.
entries.newText: Dough expanded by gas from fermentation, with bubbles held inside it.

entries.originalDescription: A fermented fruit drink, no longer the fresh juice it began as.
entries.newText: Fruit juice changed by fermentation into an alcoholic drink.

entries.originalDescription: A mineral coating for pottery; its finished surface depends on the potter's firing.
entries.newText: A coating that forms a smooth, glass-like surface when pottery is fired.

entries.originalDescription: The smith’s hot working hearth, with bellows and nearby hammer, anvil and heading tools.
entries.newText: A metalworker's hot hearth, with bellows to supply air and tools for shaping the metal.

entries.originalDescription: Workable metal: strong enough for edges, fasteners and fittings once shaped.
entries.newText: A metal that can be shaped into tools, fasteners and fittings.

entries.originalDescription: Two metal leaves joined around a pin so one side can swing relative to the other.
entries.newText: A joint that lets a door or lid swing while staying attached.

entries.originalDescription: A dark, carbon-rich material made from wood under controlled firing.
entries.newText: A carbon-rich fuel made by heating wood with limited air.

entries.originalDescription: A wooden conduit with an open passage through its length.
entries.newText: A wooden pipe with a passage through its length for water.

entries.originalDescription: A prepared coloured medium that can cover a surface with visible shapes.
entries.newText: A coloured material spread onto a surface to make an image or coating.

entries.originalDescription: Sugar stocks have a social history: plantation economies and enslaved labour helped expand European consumption.

originalReading.text:
In his 1657 account of Barbados, Richard Ligon describes a sugar plantation sale that included enslaved people among its property. His projected plantation budget treats enslaved people as assets to be maintained.

This is one record of the coerced labour behind seventeenth-century Atlantic plantation sugar. Ligon wrote from the colonists’ profit-seeking perspective, not the voices of the people they enslaved. It is not a history of every place or period in which sugar was made.
originalReading.attribution: Game-author paraphrase and contextual note, not a quotation. Richard Ligon, A True & Exact History of the Island of Barbados (1657), pp. 22–23 and 113–116. A colonial participant’s account; not testimony from enslaved workers.

entries.newText: A sweet ingredient used in preserves, cakes and confectionery. In a 1657 account of Barbados, Richard Ligon describes plantation sugar production that treated enslaved people as property. His account records the colonists' pursuit of profit, not the voices of the people they enslaved; it does not describe every place or period that made sugar.
