entries.originalDescription: An attributed historical passage about lettuce, not a dietary recommendation.

originalReading.text:
“It is indeed of Nature more cold and moist than any of the rest”

Evelyn describes lettuce through the cold-and-moist qualities of humoral dietetics. The same entry combines culinary description with claims about the body. This is a historical example of a discarded explanation, not evidence or advice about eating lettuce.
originalReading.attribution: John Evelyn, Acetaria (1699), catalogue entry 34: Lettuce. Excerpt spelling modernised; contextual note by the game author.

entries.newText:
“It is indeed of Nature more cold and moist than any of the rest”

Evelyn describes lettuce using an old medical theory that classified foods as hot, cold, wet or dry. That theory is no longer an accepted explanation of how food affects health.

entries.originalDescription: The station kitchen’s serving trolley: supper, apple juice and an unopened tin of provisions have fixed places; either finished cake can supply dessert. Every loaded dish stays visible.
entries.newText: A serving trolley with places for supper, apple juice, a sealed tin of provisions and a finished cake. The loaded dishes remain visible.

entries.originalDescription: Shared printing supplies: many blank sheets, an ink roller and ink. A proof uses one sheet; enough stock remains to try both blocks.
entries.newText: Blank paper, ink and a roller for printing. There are enough sheets to test both wooden blocks.

entries.originalDescription: The actual thin paper sheet you printed. It has upright readable RIVER followed by a right-pointing arrow, with a marked top edge. Its back is clean and the design is visible through it.
entries.newText: The paper impression reads RIVER → with its top edge marked. The thin sheet lets the design be seen through its clean back.

entries.originalDescription: A separate tracing sheet made while viewing the master through its back. The whole word and arrow are horizontally reflected; the top stays at the top.
entries.newText: A separate sheet traced through the back of the master. The whole word and arrow are reversed left to right, while the top remains at the top.

entries.originalDescription: Several prepared wooden blocks, separate carbon transfer sheets and carving tools. A drawing is kept face up over a transfer sheet whose coated side faces the wood. Tracing transfers the same viewed design. The cutter leaves those lines raised. The master is not coated or cut.

originalReading.text:
COPY A DRAWING TO WOOD
Keep the master or tracing face up over a separate carbon transfer sheet, coated side toward a fresh wooden block. Keep the top edges aligned. Trace the outlines, lift both papers, then carve away the background, leaving the same viewed design raised. Neither drawing is coated or cut.

TRACE THE BACK VIEW
At the back-lit window, hold the thin master with its printed face against the glass, top edge up. Put a fresh tracing sheet over its clean back and copy the outlines visible through it. The new guide reflects the whole word-and-arrow image. The original master stays intact. Sheets and pencils are stocked at the window.

TAKE A PROOF
Ink either block’s raised face with the roller, press a sheet onto it and lift the impression. The paper shows a reflection of the block’s face. A proof is optional; it does not use up the block. The paper pack and workbench have enough sheets, blanks and transfer sheets to try either form. The word and top mark are part of the design, not just a rotatable arrow.
originalReading.attribution: Method sheet packed with the workroom tools — fictional workshop instructions.

entries.newText:
To make a wooden copy, lay the chosen drawing face up over a separate transfer sheet and a blank block, with the top edges aligned. Trace the outlines and carve away the background. The raised wooden design matches the drawing as you viewed it. The original paper is not cut.

To make a reversed guide, hold the master against the lit window with its printed face toward the glass. Trace the design seen through its back onto a fresh sheet.

Printing reverses a block's raised face onto paper. Ink either block and take a proof to check it. The workbench has enough paper, transfer sheets and blank blocks to try both versions.

entries.originalDescription: A new wooden block with upright readable RIVER and a right arrow raised on its face. Its top edge is marked.
entries.newText: The raised wooden face reads RIVER → normally, with its top edge marked. This is the face people would read on a displayed panel.

entries.originalDescription: A new wooden block with the whole word-and-arrow image horizontally reflected on its raised face. Its top edge is marked.
entries.newText: The raised wooden face reverses the whole RIVER design from left to right. Printing will reverse it again on paper.

entries.originalDescription: A real new sheet from the paper pack, printed from the readable-faced block. The whole word and arrow appear horizontally reflected.
entries.newText: The paper impression reverses the normally readable wooden face. Both the word and the arrow are reflected.

entries.originalDescription: A real new sheet from the paper pack, printed from the reflected-faced block. It matches the earlier master.
entries.newText: The paper impression reads RIVER → normally. It was printed from the reversed wooden face and matches the earlier master.

entries.originalDescription: This invented case separates a desired good from a wrong choice. Enjoying food is not itself the wrong; taking what another is owed is.

originalReading.text: This invented case separates a desired good from a wrong choice. Enjoying food is not itself the wrong; taking what another is owed is.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial application of Augustine’s wrongly directed will, Enchiridion §§23–27.

entries.newText: Enjoying food is good, but the neighbour is still owed their share. The wrong is taking that food, not enjoying a meal.

entries.originalDescription: The body exists both before and after healing. What changes is its condition. Calling the wound a loss does not make the pain unreal.

originalReading.text: The body exists both before and after healing. What changes is its condition. Calling the wound a loss does not make the pain unreal.
originalReading.attribution: Augustine, Enchiridion §§11–12; local explanation, not a universal proof.

entries.newText: The body is still there, but its health has been damaged. Calling the wound a loss does not make its pain unreal.

entries.originalDescription: The meal and the ability to choose can be good things. The choice is defective because it puts private comfort above the neighbour’s claim.

originalReading.text: The meal and the ability to choose can be good things. The choice is defective because it puts private comfort above the neighbour’s claim.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial application of Augustine, Enchiridion §§23–27.

entries.newText: Enjoying food and being able to choose are not themselves wrong. The wrong choice is taking food that another person is owed.

entries.originalDescription: Both cases involve something missing: health in one, fairness in the other. Only the second case includes a deliberate wrongful choice. Do not turn an analogy between losses into blame for suffering.

originalReading.text: Both cases involve something missing: health in one, fairness in the other. Only the second case includes a deliberate wrongful choice. Do not turn an analogy between losses into blame for suffering.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial distinction prompted by Augustine’s bodily and moral examples.

entries.newText: A wound is harm suffered; stealing the meal is a wrong deliberately chosen. Comparing them as losses must not turn suffering into evidence of guilt.

entries.originalDescription: A wound is not a second material added to a body: it is health missing from a body. Augustine thinks evil is like that—a good thing damaged or lacking something it should have.

originalReading.text:
A wound is not a second material added to a body: it is health missing from a body. Augustine thinks evil is like that—a good thing damaged or lacking something it should have.

He begins from belief in a good creation. The wound illustrates his account; it does not prove that it explains every evil.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Augustine thinks evil is damage to, or loss of, something good rather than a separate evil material. A wound illustrates the idea: the body remains, but health is missing. His belief in a good creation is a starting point, not something the example proves.

entries.originalDescription: An invented continuation: knowing and promising have not produced the action. It illustrates a gap; it does not by itself prove why everyone fails.

originalReading.text: An invented continuation: knowing and promising have not produced the action. It illustrates a gap; it does not by itself prove why everyone fails.
originalReading.attribution: Invented case or editorial comparison, not a reported historical event.

entries.newText: The person knows they should return the food and promises to do so, then chooses comfort again. Understanding and promising have not yet produced the right action.

entries.originalDescription: Baptism is a Christian rite using water. Augustine asks why infants receive it for forgiveness. The practice is evidence for his question, not automatic proof of his answer.

originalReading.text: Baptism is a Christian rite using water. Augustine asks why infants receive it for forgiveness. The practice is evidence for his question, not automatic proof of his answer.
originalReading.attribution: Augustine, Enchiridion §§43–45.

entries.newText: Augustine's church baptizes infants for forgiveness. Because an infant has chosen no wrongful act, Augustine asks what this forgiveness addresses.

entries.originalDescription: Adam is the first human in the biblical story. Augustine says Adam’s disobedience leaves later humans needing forgiveness even before they choose a wrong act.

originalReading.text:
Adam is the first human in the biblical story. Augustine says Adam’s disobedience leaves later humans needing forgiveness even before they choose a wrong act.

This is his teaching about inherited sin, not a claim about genetics or a judgment that sick children have behaved badly.
originalReading.attribution: Augustine, Enchiridion §§26–27,45.

entries.newText: Adam is the first human in the biblical story. Augustine says Adam's disobedience leaves later humans needing forgiveness even before choosing a wrong act. For him, an infant's illness does not show that the child has behaved badly.

entries.originalDescription: The case leaves a gap between understanding and action. Augustine thinks an account of divine help must address that gap as well as ignorance.

originalReading.text: The case leaves a gap between understanding and action. Augustine thinks an account of divine help must address that gap as well as ignorance.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Knowing what is right has not been enough to make the person do it. Augustine argues that God's help must address willing and acting as well as ignorance.

entries.originalDescription: Inward help does not mean the human actor disappears. On Augustine’s account, the person really chooses and acts with help from God.

originalReading.text: Inward help does not mean the human actor disappears. On Augustine’s account, the person really chooses and acts with help from God.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Augustine says God can help a person want and do what is right. The person still chooses and acts; help does not make the human actor disappear.

entries.originalDescription: The ritual and the infant’s lack of personal acts create a question. Neither observation alone states Augustine’s doctrine of original sin.

originalReading.text: The ritual and the infant’s lack of personal acts create a question. Neither observation alone states Augustine’s doctrine of original sin.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial reconstruction of Augustine’s question, Enchiridion §§43–45.

entries.newText: The infant has chosen no wrong act, yet Augustine's church baptizes infants for forgiveness. This creates a question about what needs forgiving; the practice alone does not prove his answer.

entries.originalDescription: His premise about Adam answers the baptismal puzzle: infants share a condition needing forgiveness before they commit personal wrongs. Christians have disputed both the account and its implications.

originalReading.text: His premise about Adam answers the baptismal puzzle: infants share a condition needing forgiveness before they commit personal wrongs. Christians have disputed both the account and its implications.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Augustine says infants inherit a condition needing forgiveness through Adam, before choosing any wrong act themselves. Christians have disputed this teaching and its implications.

entries.originalDescription: For Augustine, the sick baby and the healthy baby both inherit Adam’s sinful condition. Their health is not what decides whether they need forgiveness.

originalReading.text:
For Augustine, the sick baby and the healthy baby both inherit Adam’s sinful condition. Their health is not what decides whether they need forgiveness.

Neither infant has chosen a wrong act. The comparison reconstructs Augustine’s teaching rather than blaming a child for illness.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: In Augustine's account, both the ill infant and the healthy infant inherit Adam's sinful condition. Neither has chosen a wrong act. Their health is not what determines their need for forgiveness.

entries.originalDescription: The Book of Two Principles argues that a completely good source cannot produce evil. If that rule is accepted, the world’s harms need a different source.

originalReading.text:
The Book of Two Principles argues that a completely good source cannot produce evil. If that rule is accepted, the world’s harms need a different source.

The rule is an additional claim, not something established simply by noticing suffering. Other writers on the desk dispute it.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The Book of Two Principles claims that a wholly good source cannot produce evil. That rule is an extra premise in its argument, not something proved merely by noticing suffering.

entries.originalDescription: The quotation has been given a specific causal interpretation. A reader can accept the verse while disputing that interpretation.

originalReading.text: The quotation has been given a specific causal interpretation. A reader can accept the verse while disputing that interpretation.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The writer reads the tree-and-fruit saying as a rule about the sources of good and evil. Accepting the verse does not require accepting that particular interpretation.

entries.originalDescription: The writer sees both good and harm in the world. Since the writer’s rule forbids evil coming from a wholly good source, the argument calls for opposed sources.

originalReading.text:
The writer sees both good and harm in the world. Since the writer’s rule forbids evil coming from a wholly good source, the argument calls for opposed sources.

This is one surviving medieval dualist argument. It is not a creed shared by everyone called Cathar, and completing it does not prove it true.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The writer of the Book of Two Principles sees both good and harm in the world. Because the writer holds that a wholly good source cannot cause evil, the argument requires opposed sources. This conflicts with Augustine's account of evil as damaged goodness.

entries.originalDescription: The response about an observer does not yet remove the maker’s responsibility. The point challenges an inference; it does not by itself establish two creators.

originalReading.text: The response about an observer does not yet remove the maker’s responsibility. The point challenges an inference; it does not by itself establish two creators.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Knowing that harm will happen is different from making the conditions that cause it. A reply about a passive observer does not fully answer the question about a knowing creator.

entries.originalDescription: Augustine explains evil as loss within created good. This medieval writer gives evil an opposed origin. Putting the accounts side by side identifies disagreement without staging an imaginary meeting.

originalReading.text: Augustine explains evil as loss within created good. This medieval writer gives evil an opposed origin. Putting the accounts side by side identifies disagreement without staging an imaginary meeting.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Augustine says evil is damage within a good creation. The writer of the Book of Two Principles argues that a wholly good source cannot cause evil, so evil must have an opposed source. The two accounts give different answers to the same problem of suffering and wrongdoing.

entries.originalDescription: Aquinas calls a thing good in one respect when it successfully acts according to its nature. This does not mean the fire is morally virtuous. His example asks whether effective action can still harm something else.

originalReading.text: Aquinas calls a thing good in one respect when it successfully acts according to its nature. This does not mean the fire is morally virtuous. His example asks whether effective action can still harm something else.
originalReading.attribution: Aquinas, Summa I q.49 a.1.

entries.newText: For Aquinas, fire functions well as fire when it heats and burns. That does not make it morally good or mean that every effect is good for everything nearby.

entries.originalDescription: Aquinas imagines fire doing its own job successfully while destroying water. Something can work well as the thing it is and still harm something else.

originalReading.text:
Aquinas imagines fire doing its own job successfully while destroying water. Something can work well as the thing it is and still harm something else.

He describes the destruction of water’s form: what makes it water. This is his medieval natural philosophy, not a modern chemistry lesson.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Aquinas imagines fire working according to its nature while destroying water. His medieval account concerns the loss of what makes it water, not a modern chemistry explanation.

entries.originalDescription: The fire example distinguishes good functioning from every consequence being good for everything. It challenges an undifferentiated rule that a good cause produces no evil effects.

originalReading.text: The fire example distinguishes good functioning from every consequence being good for everything. It challenges an undifferentiated rule that a good cause produces no evil effects.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Fire can function well as fire while harming something else. This challenges a rule that treats good functioning and harmless effects as the same thing.

entries.originalDescription: The example offers an alternative to the earlier inference to opposed origins. It is not a complete answer to every question about suffering or a creator’s responsibility.

originalReading.text: The example offers an alternative to the earlier inference to opposed origins. It is not a complete answer to every question about suffering or a creator’s responsibility.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Aquinas's example offers a way for harmful effects to come from something functioning well. It challenges the need for a separate evil source without answering every question about suffering.

entries.originalDescription: Aquinas allows reasoning within theology without pretending that creatures demonstrate the Trinity. Keep explanation, evidence and starting belief distinct.

originalReading.text: Aquinas allows reasoning within theology without pretending that creatures demonstrate the Trinity. Keep explanation, evidence and starting belief distinct.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Aquinas distinguishes explaining a belief from proving it. He allows reasoning about the Trinity while denying that observations of created things can establish it.

entries.originalDescription: The fire example challenges the claim that every harmful effect needs a wholly evil source. A thing may cause harm while doing what belongs to its nature.

originalReading.text:
The fire example challenges the claim that every harmful effect needs a wholly evil source. A thing may cause harm while doing what belongs to its nature.

That leaves another question open: why would a knowing creator make a world where such harm happens? This answer does not solve every problem of suffering.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The fire example challenges the claim that every harmful effect needs a wholly evil source. It still leaves the question of why a knowing creator would make a world in which such harm occurs.

entries.originalDescription: A human can be someone’s teacher without belonging to a different kind of being from the pupil. This limited comparison concerns how words work; it is not a model of the Trinity.

originalReading.text: A human can be someone’s teacher without belonging to a different kind of being from the pupil. This limited comparison concerns how words work; it is not a model of the Trinity.
originalReading.attribution: Invented case or editorial comparison, not a reported historical event.

entries.newText: A teacher and pupil have different roles while both remaining human. A difference in relationship does not automatically mean a difference in the kind of being they are.

entries.originalDescription: The text presents the Son addressing the Father. Augustine’s account must preserve distinction as well as unity; the verse is not a complete proof of his account.

originalReading.text: The text presents the Son addressing the Father. Augustine’s account must preserve distinction as well as unity; the verse is not a complete proof of his account.
originalReading.attribution: John 17:1, King James Version (public domain), four-word quotation; the ellipsis marks omitted words.

entries.newText: The Son addresses the Father. Augustine must explain how this real relationship belongs within his belief in one God.

entries.originalDescription: The teacher example shows why a difference of title is not automatically a difference of nature. Augustine applies that distinction to Father and Son without making God a human family.

originalReading.text: The teacher example shows why a difference of title is not automatically a difference of nature. Augustine applies that distinction to Father and Son without making God a human family.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Teacher and pupil have different roles while both being human. Augustine similarly treats Father and Son as names of a relationship, not names for greater and lesser kinds of God.

entries.originalDescription: The proposed inference fails: a relational name does not automatically grade the kind of being. Augustine still needs his positive beliefs about divine unity and distinction.

originalReading.text: The proposed inference fails: a relational name does not automatically grade the kind of being. Augustine still needs his positive beliefs about divine unity and distinction.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Calling someone Son describes a relationship; it does not by itself mean a lesser kind of being. This clarifies Augustine's argument without proving his beliefs about divine unity.

entries.originalDescription: Three people are all human, but they are still three separate beings. Augustine does not mean that Father, Son and Spirit are three similar gods.

originalReading.text:
Three people are all human, but they are still three separate beings. Augustine does not mean that Father, Son and Spirit are three similar gods.

His claim is one divine being, with real distinctions. The human comparison shows what he is not saying; it does not demonstrate his belief.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Three humans share a kind but remain three separate beings. Augustine's claim is different: Father, Son and Spirit are one divine being with real distinctions, not three similar gods.

entries.originalDescription: The Son addresses the Father. Within Augustine’s account, unity does not erase this relation. Father, Son and Spirit are not successive costumes worn by an otherwise undifferentiated actor.

originalReading.text: The Son addresses the Father. Within Augustine’s account, unity does not erase this relation. Father, Son and Spirit are not successive costumes worn by an otherwise undifferentiated actor.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: In Augustine's account, Father and Son are genuinely distinct: the Son addresses the Father. They are not one actor successively wearing different costumes.

entries.originalDescription: The Trinity means Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one God. The three are not lesser and greater gods, three similar gods, or one actor changing costumes.

originalReading.text:
The Trinity means Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one God. The three are not lesser and greater gods, three similar gods, or one actor changing costumes.

These comparisons clarify the claim. Aquinas still says ordinary reasoning from the world cannot prove it.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The Trinity means one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The claim is not three similar gods, greater and lesser gods, or one actor changing roles. The comparisons clarify the belief without proving it.

entries.originalDescription: The rite claims forgiveness of sins and reception of the Holy Spirit—God dwelling with the believer. It calls this spiritual baptism rather than washing with water. These are its claims, not events the game verifies.

originalReading.text: The rite claims forgiveness of sins and reception of the Holy Spirit—God dwelling with the believer. It calls this spiritual baptism rather than washing with water. These are its claims, not events the game verifies.
originalReading.attribution: Lyon ritual III.22–31; IV.3,18–21,49–53; original paraphrase.

entries.newText: The Lyon rite promises forgiveness and the Holy Spirit, understood as God dwelling with the believer. It calls the laying on of hands spiritual baptism rather than washing with water.

entries.originalDescription: The pledge concerns a demanding pattern of life. Do not silently replace “worldly desires” with a complete statement about who created matter.

originalReading.text: The pledge concerns a demanding pattern of life. Do not silently replace “worldly desires” with a complete statement about who created matter.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The candidate promises to turn away from “worldly desires”. This concerns how the person should live; it does not state a complete explanation of who created matter.

entries.originalDescription: The ritual invokes enemy-love as part of the candidate’s obligations. Renunciation here cannot mean that other people no longer matter.

originalReading.text: The ritual invokes enemy-love as part of the candidate’s obligations. Renunciation here cannot mean that other people no longer matter.
originalReading.attribution: Matthew 5:44, King James Version (public domain), three-word quotation; compare ritual IV.32.

entries.newText: Loving enemies is one of the candidate's obligations. Turning away from worldly desires therefore cannot mean abandoning concern for other people.

entries.originalDescription: The Lyon ritual points to Acts, where Jesus’s first followers lay hands on believers who receive the Holy Spirit. Its ministers claim to continue that practice.

originalReading.text:
The Lyon ritual points to Acts, where Jesus’s first followers lay hands on believers who receive the Holy Spirit. Its ministers claim to continue that practice.

The technical word is apostolic: connected to the apostles. This explains the rite’s authority claim; it does not independently verify a chain of transmission.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The Lyon ritual appeals to the laying on of hands described among Jesus's first followers. Its ministers claim authority by continuing that practice.

entries.originalDescription: The candidate’s body, the ministers’ hands and the book are not absent. Physical action and a claimed spiritual effect are not simple opposites.

originalReading.text: The candidate’s body, the ministers’ hands and the book are not absent. Physical action and a claimed spiritual effect are not simple opposites.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The ritual uses a person's body, ministers' hands and a Gospel book while claiming a spiritual gift. Physical action and a claimed inward effect are not simple opposites.

entries.originalDescription: Hands and a book show that this rite uses bodies. They do not tell us whether its community believed in one good creator or opposed sources of good and evil.

originalReading.text:
Hands and a book show that this rite uses bodies. They do not tell us whether its community believed in one good creator or opposed sources of good and evil.

The Lyon ritual and the Book of Two Principles are different surviving texts. Their claims must not be merged into one universal Cathar doctrine.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Hands and a book show that the rite uses physical objects. They do not establish whether its community believed in one good creator or opposed sources. The Lyon ritual and the Book of Two Principles must not be merged into one universal Cathar doctrine.

entries.originalDescription: The two obligations give renunciation concrete moral content. The candidate is not being told that other people’s treatment is irrelevant.

originalReading.text: The two obligations give renunciation concrete moral content. The candidate is not being told that other people’s treatment is irrelevant.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The candidate promises to reject worldly desires and to love enemies. Giving up those desires does not remove duties toward other people.

entries.originalDescription: Here grace means God’s gift of help, and nature means human powers such as reasoning and willing—not the countryside. Aquinas says that help fulfils those powers rather than wiping them out.

originalReading.text:
Here grace means God’s gift of help, and nature means human powers such as reasoning and willing—not the countryside. Aquinas says that help fulfils those powers rather than wiping them out.

His immediate example is reason serving faith, and he also compares willing and love. Perfecting is not a promise that a person becomes incapable of error. Comparing this with Augustine’s aided actor does not settle every question about free choice.
originalReading.attribution: Aquinas, Summa I q.1 a.8, reply 2; eight-word quotation from the public-domain English translation.

entries.newText: God's gift of help develops human powers such as reasoning and willing rather than erasing them. Aquinas describes reason serving faith and willing guided by love. This does not mean a person becomes incapable of error, and questions about free choice remain.

entries.originalDescription: The axe really cuts, but the craftsperson makes the bed through it. Both act; the axe is not a second independent craftsperson.

originalReading.text:
The axe really cuts, but the craftsperson makes the bed through it. Both act; the axe is not a second independent craftsperson.

This is Aquinas’s comparison for an instrument: something through which another acts. The comparison does not prove that a religious rite works.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The axe cuts the wood, while the craftsperson makes the bed through it. Both act, but the axe is not a second independent maker. Aquinas uses this pattern to explain how God could act through a rite.

entries.originalDescription: A tool can really act while another works through it. Aquinas uses that pattern to explain how a rite could give grace while God remains its source.

originalReading.text:
A tool can really act while another works through it. Aquinas uses that pattern to explain how a rite could give grace while God remains its source.

This answers the objection that the rite would rival God. It does not yet establish that God appointed this particular rite.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Aquinas argues that God can act through a rite as a craftsperson acts through a tool. This explains how the rite need not rival God, but does not prove that God appointed any particular ceremony.

entries.originalDescription: Ordinary water does not acquire a rival divine power. His claim combines an instituted rite with God’s action.

originalReading.text: Ordinary water does not acquire a rival divine power. His claim combines an instituted rite with God’s action.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Aquinas believes God chose baptism with water to give inward grace. The water acts through God's choice; it does not gain independent divine power.

entries.originalDescription: For Aquinas, baptism’s water washes the body while God works through the rite to cleanse the soul. The water is an instrument: God’s tool, not a second god.

originalReading.text:
For Aquinas, baptism’s water washes the body while God works through the rite to cleanse the soul. The water is an instrument: God’s tool, not a second god.

The tool comparison explains the claim. Belief that God appointed baptism supplies the further premise; ordinary water is not automatically a sacrament.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: For Aquinas, baptism washes the body while God works through the rite to give inward grace. The water is God's instrument, not a second god. This depends on his further belief that God appointed baptism; ordinary water is not automatically a sacrament.

entries.originalDescription: Augustine’s person still chooses; Aquinas’s instrument still acts. This is a limited comparison of dependent action, not an assertion that persons are merely tools.

originalReading.text: Augustine’s person still chooses; Aquinas’s instrument still acts. This is a limited comparison of dependent action, not an assertion that persons are merely tools.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Augustine's helped person still chooses, and Aquinas's tool still acts. The comparison shows that dependent action can be real; it does not mean people are merely tools.

entries.originalDescription: The Lyon rite uses hands and a Gospel book; Aquinas discusses baptism with water. Both claim inward gifts through bodily actions.

originalReading.text:
The Lyon rite uses hands and a Gospel book; Aquinas discusses baptism with water. Both claim inward gifts through bodily actions.

That resemblance does not make them the same rite. They appeal to different claims about which practice God authorized and how it gives the gift.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The Lyon rite uses hands and a Gospel book; Aquinas discusses baptism with water. Both claim an inward gift through physical actions, but disagree about the authorized rite and how it gives that gift.

entries.originalDescription: Imagine a participant reporting the same taste, colour and shape. This is an observation in an invented case, not evidence that a miracle has or has not occurred.

originalReading.text: Imagine a participant reporting the same taste, colour and shape. This is an observation in an invented case, not evidence that a miracle has or has not occurred.
originalReading.attribution: Invented case or editorial comparison, not a reported historical event.

entries.newText: After the blessing, the bread looks and tastes the same. Aquinas's account must explain why he still says that what it is has changed.

entries.originalDescription: Looking and tasting tell us how something appears. Aquinas says that, in Communion, those appearances can stay while what the thing is changes.

originalReading.text:
Looking and tasting tell us how something appears. Aquinas says that, in Communion, those appearances can stay while what the thing is changes.

He calls what it is its substance, and the remaining qualities its accidents. These are his philosophical terms, not a claim that tasting proves a miracle.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Aquinas distinguishes what something is from its appearance. In Communion, he says the bread's substance—what it is—changes, while qualities such as taste and colour remain. He calls those remaining qualities accidents.

entries.originalDescription: The reading adds a specific claim to the biblical words. Reconstructing the reading does not make it the only possible interpretation.

originalReading.text: The reading adds a specific claim to the biblical words. Reconstructing the reading does not make it the only possible interpretation.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Aquinas reads Christ's supper words as saying that bread becomes Christ's body. This is a particular interpretation, not the only possible reading established by the words alone.

entries.originalDescription: The observation and the doctrine address different aspects. This distinction explains why the two do not directly contradict within Aquinas’s account; it does not verify the account.

originalReading.text: The observation and the doctrine address different aspects. This distinction explains why the two do not directly contradict within Aquinas’s account; it does not verify the account.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Aquinas says the appearance stays the same while what the thing is changes. Unchanged taste therefore does not contradict his account, but it does not verify it either.

entries.originalDescription: Aquinas holds both claims together: what was bread becomes Christ’s body, and the familiar look and taste remain. That is his account of Communion, also called the Eucharist.

originalReading.text:
Aquinas holds both claims together: what was bread becomes Christ’s body, and the familiar look and taste remain. That is his account of Communion, also called the Eucharist.

The technical name is transubstantiation. Reconstructing the account explains what he means; it does not establish that the change occurred.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Aquinas says the bread becomes Christ's body while keeping the look and taste of bread. This is called transubstantiation. Explaining the claim about Communion does not establish that the change occurred.

entries.originalDescription: Unchanged taste is compatible with Aquinas’s claim because he says the appearances remain. But compatibility is not proof: tasting cannot establish the hidden change.

originalReading.text:
Unchanged taste is compatible with Aquinas’s claim because he says the appearances remain. But compatibility is not proof: tasting cannot establish the hidden change.

Aquinas rests the claim on faith in divine authority. This reuses the earlier distinction between explaining a belief and demonstrating it.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Tasting the bread cannot prove the change Aquinas describes, because he says its taste remains. His account rests on faith in divine authority, not on a hidden change detected by the senses.

entries.originalDescription: “Matter matters” would be too vague. One account gives water a dependent action; the other says what was bread changes while appearances remain.

originalReading.text: “Matter matters” would be too vague. One account gives water a dependent action; the other says what was bread changes while appearances remain.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: For Aquinas, baptism's water is a tool through which God acts. In Communion, what was bread becomes Christ's body while appearances remain. These give physical things different roles.

entries.originalDescription: A fictional household must choose what to do with scarce money. No historical family is claimed here. The competing need makes the moral cost of a purchase visible.

originalReading.text: A fictional household must choose what to do with scarce money. No historical family is claimed here. The competing need makes the moral cost of a purchase visible.
originalReading.attribution: Invented case or editorial comparison, not a reported historical event.

entries.newText: The household has one coin and no supper. Spending it on an indulgence would leave the family's immediate need for food unmet.

entries.originalDescription: A promise of certain release based on money crosses the distinction between a limited church act and control over God’s mercy.

originalReading.text: A promise of certain release based on money crosses the distinction between a limited church act and control over God’s mercy.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Luther rejects a seller's guarantee that a payment will release a dead soul. A limited church role does not give the seller control over God's mercy.

entries.originalDescription: The household’s need gives the general priority a concrete consequence. This is an editorial application of Luther’s stated rule, not an event from his biography.

originalReading.text: The household’s need gives the general priority a concrete consequence. This is an editorial application of Luther’s stated rule, not an event from his biography.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Luther gives household necessities and help for poor neighbours priority over buying an indulgence. With one coin and no supper, the household should buy food first.

entries.originalDescription: A person can serve God without controlling God. The earlier baptism argument helps distinguish a dependent role from power to make God forgive for money.

originalReading.text:
A person can serve God without controlling God. The earlier baptism argument helps distinguish a dependent role from power to make God forgive for money.

This is a comparison of limits, not a claim that Luther’s account of the pope and Aquinas’s account of baptism are identical.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: A person can serve God without controlling God's gifts. Comparing Luther's limits on church authority with Aquinas's dependent instrument clarifies that distinction without making their doctrines identical.

entries.originalDescription: The sales claim is now tested against both the letter’s limit and repentance. The result is not a blanket declaration that every church rite or payment is fraudulent.

originalReading.text: The sales claim is now tested against both the letter’s limit and repentance. The result is not a blanket declaration that every church rite or payment is fraudulent.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: For Luther, a guarantee based on payment cannot replace repentance and a changed life. This criticism is not a blanket claim that every church rite or payment is fraudulent.

entries.originalDescription: If feeding someone cannot buy God’s acceptance, it can still feed a hungry person. Not earning salvation does not make the action pointless.

originalReading.text:
If feeding someone cannot buy God’s acceptance, it can still feed a hungry person. Not earning salvation does not make the action pointless.

Luther changes the reason for service: it answers another person’s need instead of presenting God with a bill.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Feeding someone can help them even if it does not earn acceptance by God. Luther gives service a purpose in the neighbour's need rather than treating it as a payment for salvation.

entries.originalDescription: The act is no longer a price demanded for acceptance. Its direction changes: toward the neighbour’s need, following Christ’s service.

originalReading.text: The act is no longer a price demanded for acceptance. Its direction changes: toward the neighbour’s need, following Christ’s service.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Luther calls for service because the neighbour needs help, following Christ's freely given service. The deed is not a price paid to earn God's acceptance.

entries.originalDescription: The household still needs supper. Luther’s account gives the meal a clear purpose—helping people—without making it a payment for being accepted by God.

originalReading.text:
The household still needs supper. Luther’s account gives the meal a clear purpose—helping people—without making it a payment for being accepted by God.

This reuses the earlier choice about the household’s coin. It is an editorial application of his 1520 argument, not a reported event in his life.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The household still needs supper. For Luther, feeding them serves that need without buying acceptance by God. A good deed can matter to other people without becoming payment for salvation.

entries.originalDescription: Augustine’s case asks how someone comes to want and do what is right. Luther’s case asks what makes someone right with God.

originalReading.text:
Augustine’s case asks how someone comes to want and do what is right. Luther’s case asks what makes someone right with God.

Both concern God’s gift, often called grace. The questions overlap, but an answer about help with choosing is not yet an account of faith and justification.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Augustine asks how God helps a person want and do what is right. Luther asks what makes a person right with God. Both concern God's gift, but answering one question does not fully answer the other.

entries.originalDescription: Luther still gives bodily work and discipline a job: training a person for life and service. It is not a way to buy acceptance by God.

originalReading.text:
Luther still gives bodily work and discipline a job: training a person for life and service. It is not a way to buy acceptance by God.

So the choice is not between earning salvation and doing nothing. Effort can matter without becoming the price of the gift.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: For Luther, bodily work and discipline can train a person for service. Effort matters without becoming the price of God's acceptance.

entries.originalDescription: A sign can bring someone to mind without containing that person’s body. Zwingli uses this kind of example in his supper argument; it illustrates a reading rather than proving it.

originalReading.text: A sign can bring someone to mind without containing that person’s body. Zwingli uses this kind of example in his supper argument; it illustrates a reading rather than proving it.
originalReading.attribution: Zwingli, On the Lord’s Supper (1526), Third Article; original paraphrase, not a quotation of the modern translation.

entries.newText: A ring can bring a loved person to mind without containing their body. Zwingli uses this example to explain how Communion's bread can point to Christ without containing his body.

entries.originalDescription: Spiritual reception means sharing in Christ through faith, not deciding where his body is. Article 15 affirms that reception and the supper’s strengthening of faith, while recording disagreement about bodily presence in bread and wine. It supplies no shared physical mechanism.

originalReading.text: Spiritual reception means sharing in Christ through faith, not deciding where his body is. Article 15 affirms that reception and the supper’s strengthening of faith, while recording disagreement about bodily presence in bread and wine. It supplies no shared physical mechanism.
originalReading.attribution: Marburg Articles, article 15; “through faith” is a plain-language gloss read with articles 5–8, not a quoted common mechanism.

entries.newText: The signers affirm receiving Christ through faith and the supper's strengthening of faith. They still disagree about Christ's bodily presence in bread and wine; they do not share one account of how that presence works.

entries.originalDescription: Luther says the unbelieving guest still receives Christ’s body. But receiving it without trusting the promise does not bring the promised forgiveness.

originalReading.text:
Luther says the unbelieving guest still receives Christ’s body. But receiving it without trusting the promise does not bring the promised forgiveness.

He distinguishes what is given from its benefit to the receiver. This reconstructs Luther’s account rather than deciding which writer is right.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Luther says an unbelieving Communion guest still receives Christ's body with the bread, because Christ's words establish the gift. Without trusting the promise, the guest does not receive its promised forgiveness. What is given and its benefit to the receiver are separate questions.

entries.originalDescription: Your earlier clarified doctrine can be genuinely shared while a different question divides these writers. Disagreement need not mean that nothing is held in common.

originalReading.text: Your earlier clarified doctrine can be genuinely shared while a different question divides these writers. Disagreement need not mean that nothing is held in common.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The writers can share belief in one God as Father, Son and Spirit while disagreeing about Communion. Real agreement does not require agreement on every question.

entries.originalDescription: The council begins with a call and help that the person has not earned. Its account is not “people start by saving themselves”.

originalReading.text: The council begins with a call and help that the person has not earned. Its account is not “people start by saving themselves”.
originalReading.attribution: Trent, Session VI, chapter V.

entries.newText: Trent begins with God's help, which the person has not earned. Its account does not say that people start by saving themselves.

entries.originalDescription: The council gives the adult a real, grace-assisted response. This is not a claim that unaided choice earns the initial gift.

originalReading.text: The council gives the adult a real, grace-assisted response. This is not a claim that unaided choice earns the initial gift.
originalReading.attribution: Session VI, chapters V–VI.

entries.newText: Trent says an adult can accept or refuse help that God gives first. The person's response is real, while the first gift remains unearned.

entries.originalDescription: God’s first help and a real human response belong to one account. The earlier Augustine distinction prevents “helped” from meaning “no human action”.

originalReading.text: God’s first help and a real human response belong to one account. The earlier Augustine distinction prevents “helped” from meaning “no human action”.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: In Trent's account, God's help comes first and a person really responds. Receiving help does not mean there is no human action.

entries.originalDescription: The adult can assent or refuse. In this account, neither real agency nor preceding help erases the other; whether the response earns anything is a further question.

originalReading.text: The adult can assent or refuse. In this account, neither real agency nor preceding help erases the other; whether the response earns anything is a further question.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Trent says the adult can accept or refuse God's prior help. Having a real choice does not mean the response earns the gift.

entries.originalDescription: The Council of Trent describes adults genuinely responding to God’s prior help. That response does not earn their first being made right with God.

originalReading.text:
The Council of Trent describes adults genuinely responding to God’s prior help. That response does not earn their first being made right with God.

This is the initial gift of justification, not a claim about infants or every later role of good deeds. The comparison concerns real response versus earning; it does not infer a requirement merely from the ability to refuse.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Trent describes an adult responding to God's help without earning the initial gift of being made right with God. This addresses initial justification, not every later role of good deeds.

entries.originalDescription: In this household case, both accounts deny that feeding someone buys our first being made right with God. That is a real, limited point of agreement.

originalReading.text:
In this household case, both accounts deny that feeding someone buys our first being made right with God. That is a real, limited point of agreement.

It does not mean Luther and Trent give the same account of faith, inward renewal, or later good deeds.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: In this household case, both accounts deny that feeding someone buys the initial gift of being made right with God. That limited agreement does not make their accounts of faith, inner renewal and later deeds identical.

entries.originalDescription: Trent says grace-enabled deeds increase the righteousness God has already given, including inward renewal. Luther’s text denies that deeds make an already-Christian person more holy before God, while still valuing bodily training and service.

originalReading.text:
Trent says grace-enabled deeds increase the righteousness God has already given, including inward renewal. Luther’s text denies that deeds make an already-Christian person more holy before God, while still valuing bodily training and service.

The dispute concerns how deeds contribute to a person’s life before God. It is not simply about whether behaviour can improve, and it does not assume their accounts of righteousness are identical in every other respect.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Trent says deeds made possible by God's help increase the righteousness already received, including inward renewal. Luther's text denies that deeds make an already-Christian person more holy before God, while valuing training and service. The disagreement is about the role of deeds before God, not merely whether behaviour improves.

entries.originalDescription: His insistence on Christ’s unique role does not mean that Christians may never ask a living neighbour for prayer.

originalReading.text: His insistence on Christ’s unique role does not mean that Christians may never ask a living neighbour for prayer.
originalReading.attribution: Calvin, Institutes III.20 §19.

entries.newText: Calvin allows Christians to ask a living neighbour to pray. He does not think this replaces Christ's unique role between people and God.

entries.originalDescription: An invented painted scene shows Stephen’s steadfastness. The proposal concerns honour in a chapel, not whether any historical picture may exist. It is not a known surviving artwork.

originalReading.text: An invented painted scene shows Stephen’s steadfastness. The proposal concerns honour in a chapel, not whether any historical picture may exist. It is not a known surviving artwork.
originalReading.attribution: Invented case or editorial comparison, not a reported historical event.

entries.newText: The proposed chapel painting shows Stephen remaining faithful. The question is whether people should direct religious honour through it, not whether all paintings should be forbidden.

entries.originalDescription: This is an evidential distinction, not a theological verdict. Even a tradition allowing relics would still need reasons to identify this particular fragment.

originalReading.text: This is an evidential distinction, not a theological verdict. Even a tradition allowing relics would still need reasons to identify this particular fragment.
originalReading.attribution: Invented case or editorial comparison, not a reported historical event.

entries.newText: A name on a label states whose bone someone claims this is. It does not prove the identity. Even a tradition that permits relics still needs evidence about this particular object.

entries.originalDescription: Calvin’s criticism has more than one level: doubtful claims and the practice of veneration itself. Solving authenticity would not automatically solve his doctrinal objection.

originalReading.text: Calvin’s criticism has more than one level: doubtful claims and the practice of veneration itself. Solving authenticity would not automatically solve his doctrinal objection.
originalReading.attribution: Calvin, Treatise on Relics, conclusion around printed p.278; distinguish his text from the translator’s preliminary dissertation.

entries.newText: Calvin objects both to doubtful relic claims and to giving relics religious honour. Establishing a bone's identity would not answer his objection to the practice.

entries.originalDescription: Asking the friend and relying on Christ need not be opposites in Calvin’s account. This establishes only the living-friend case.

originalReading.text: Asking the friend and relying on Christ need not be opposites in Calvin’s account. This establishes only the living-friend case.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Calvin permits asking a living friend to pray while relying on Christ. This answers the living-friend case, not every proposed request for help.

originalReading.text: The form of words resembles the friend request, but Calvin challenges the move across death. The petitioner’s intention does not supply his missing authority.

entries.newText: Calvin argues that Scripture does not authorize asking departed saints for prayer and that doing so obscures Christ's unique work for people before God. Calling the saint a helper does not answer these objections.

entries.originalDescription: Calvin objects to using this painting for religious honour. He does not reject every painted picture simply because it contains paint.

originalReading.text:
Calvin objects to using this painting for religious honour. He does not reject every painted picture simply because it contains paint.

The case is an invented proposal for a chapel, not an actual ruling on a surviving work of art.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: Calvin rejects giving this painting a role in religious honour. His objection concerns its use in worship, not the existence of every painted picture.

entries.originalDescription: There is not enough evidence to move from a written name to an authenticated relic. The proper result of this case is uncertainty, not a game-certified saint’s bone.

originalReading.text: The council affirms the continuing prayer of saints and recommends invoking their help. This is its religious teaching, not evidence the game can independently verify.

entries.newText: Trent teaches that saints with Christ continue to pray for people on Earth. The council therefore recommends asking for their help.

entries.newText: A new record identifies some of the people who kept the bone. It strengthens the investigation, but gaps in its history remain and a bishop has not recognized it as a relic.

entries.originalDescription: Trent says the saints pray through Christ, not as other saviours. Calvin rejects invoking them: he argues that it obscures Christ’s sole mediation as well as lacking scriptural warrant. Stating Trent’s intention does not settle Calvin’s objection.

originalReading.text: Trent says the saints pray through Christ, not as other saviours. Calvin rejects invoking them: he argues that it obscures Christ’s sole mediation as well as lacking scriptural warrant. Stating Trent’s intention does not settle Calvin’s objection.
originalReading.attribution: Trent, Session XXV; Calvin, Institutes III.20 §§19–21,27. Editorial comparison, not an agreed account of mediation.

entries.newText: Trent says saints pray through Christ rather than replacing him. Calvin still rejects asking them, arguing that it lacks biblical permission and obscures Christ's unique role. Explaining Trent's intention does not settle the disagreement.

entries.originalDescription: Directed honour provides a category the fictional proposal could occupy. It is neither divine paint nor a sacrament; no installation approval has been invented.

originalReading.text: Directed honour provides a category the fictional proposal could occupy. It is neither divine paint nor a sacrament; no installation approval has been invented.

entries.newText: Trent allows honour to pass through a painting to the person shown. The proposed Stephen painting fits that kind of use; the paint itself is not treated as divine.

originalReading.text: A doctrinal reason to honour genuine relics cannot supply the missing evidence that this particular object is one.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: A reason to honour genuine relics does not establish that this fragment is genuine. The object's identity still needs evidence.

originalReading.text: The requirement adds a procedural boundary to the evidential one. The game cannot turn a label or its own successful combination into recognition by a bishop.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: The claim about this bone still needs examination and a bishop's recognition. A name on its label and a partial history are not enough.

entries.originalDescription: A record of who kept the bone gives investigators new evidence. It does not by itself show that every link is sound or that a bishop has approved the relic.

originalReading.text:
A record of who kept the bone gives investigators new evidence. It does not by itself show that every link is sound or that a bishop has approved the relic.

The bone and record are fictional. More evidence can matter without ending an inquiry.
