entries.newText: The new record helps trace who kept the bone. It does not verify every link in its history or amount to a bishop's approval.

entries.originalDescription: A better history may strengthen the claim that this is Stephen’s bone. Calvin would still reject religious honour to it, even if its identity were established.

originalReading.text:
A better history may strengthen the claim that this is Stephen’s bone. Calvin would still reject religious honour to it, even if its identity were established.

Two questions remain separate: whose bone is it, and should such a bone receive this honour? Evidence about the first does not settle the second.
originalReading.attribution: Attributed paraphrase and editorial explanation; see the named source.

entries.newText: A better history could support the bone's claimed identity, but Calvin would still reject religious honour to it. Whose bone it is and whether it should be venerated are different questions.

entries.originalDescription: The invented pair varies bodily health while keeping the absence of a chosen offence the same. Does the illness identify who needs forgiveness?

originalReading.text: The invented pair varies bodily health while keeping the absence of a chosen offence the same. Does the illness identify who needs forgiveness?
originalReading.attribution: Editorial case or comparison, not a reported historical event.

entries.newText: One infant is ill and the other is well. Neither has chosen a wrongful act. Does either child's health determine a need for forgiveness?

entries.originalDescription: Your earlier distinction rules out reading the ill infant’s condition as evidence of a personally chosen wrong. The healthy infant has not chosen wrong either.

originalReading.text: Your earlier distinction rules out reading the ill infant’s condition as evidence of a personally chosen wrong. The healthy infant has not chosen wrong either.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial case or comparison, not a reported historical event.

entries.newText: Neither infant has chosen a wrong act. Illness in one child is not evidence that the child deliberately did wrong.

entries.originalDescription: The distinction between guilt and remaining penalties explains what an indulgence concerns. Luther’s further authority limit explains why a papal letter cannot by its own power command God’s treatment of a departed soul.

originalReading.text: The distinction between guilt and remaining penalties explains what an indulgence concerns. Luther’s further authority limit explains why a papal letter cannot by its own power command God’s treatment of a departed soul.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial reconstruction of Luther’s Ninety-Five Theses 5–7,21,27–28.

entries.newText: An indulgence concerns penalties remaining after forgiveness. Luther further limits church authority: a papal letter cannot by its own power command God to release a dead soul.

entries.originalDescription: The identity question is unresolved, but Calvin’s stated objection does not depend on resolving it. Authenticity and permission to venerate are distinct questions.

originalReading.text: The identity question is unresolved, but Calvin’s stated objection does not depend on resolving it. Authenticity and permission to venerate are distinct questions.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial application of Calvin’s authentic-or-false distinction to the fictional fragment.

entries.newText: The bone's identity remains unresolved, but Calvin's objection to honouring it does not depend on that uncertainty. A genuine object can still be disputed as a religious practice.

entries.originalDescription: The fictional record gives the investigation something new. Its incomplete custody history does not automatically authenticate the fragment or count as a bishop’s recognition.

originalReading.text: The fictional record gives the investigation something new. Its incomplete custody history does not automatically authenticate the fragment or count as a bishop’s recognition.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial case or comparison, not a reported historical event.

entries.newText: The record adds evidence about the fragment's past. Its incomplete history does not yet establish the bone's identity or supply a bishop's approval.

originalReading.text: The opening asks which people count as neighbors. Jesus’ closing question asks which character acted as a neighbor. Comparing the questions changes what a satisfactory answer looks like.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The opening asks which people count as neighbours. Jesus's closing question asks which character acted as a neighbour. The focus changes from classifying people to examining their actions.

originalReading.text: The panel holds two discoveries together: the Samaritan’s care unsettles a group boundary, and care for the stranger is not foreign to Jewish Scripture. Neither insight requires treating Judaism as a failed version of Christianity.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The Samaritan helps across a religious boundary, while Jewish Scripture already teaches care for strangers. These points do not require portraying Judaism as lacking mercy or as a failed version of Christianity.

originalReading.text: The repeated movement matters: the father runs toward one son and goes out to the other. The story’s attention is not confined to the son who returns from far away.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The father runs toward the returning son and goes outside to the angry son. His care is directed toward both, not only the son who came home.

originalReading.text: The younger son has imagined a hired servant’s place. The father’s greeting comes before the spoken request can become a contract. This reading notices the scene’s order; it does not say the son’s change of heart is irrelevant.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The younger son imagines returning as a hired servant, but the father welcomes him before such an arrangement is made. The order of the scene matters without making the son's change of heart irrelevant.

originalReading.text: The older son speaks of years of service and an unequal celebration. The father answers with continued belonging and calls the other son his brother. The complaint about fairness is heard, not simply deleted.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The older son complains that his years of service have not earned a celebration. The father answers that he still belongs and that the returning son is his brother. The complaint is heard, not simply ignored.

originalReading.text: The father goes out to the angry brother as well as to the returning son. If the older brother echoes the opening critics, the story may invite those critics to share the welcome rather than merely condemn them.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The father goes out to invite the angry older brother as well as welcoming the returning son. Read alongside the opening complaint about Jesus's meals, this may invite the critics to join the welcome.

originalReading.text: The younger son’s imagined job and the older son’s service account do not determine the celebration. The father describes someone lost being found. This is about the scene’s explanation of the feast, not a complete Christian doctrine of salvation.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The father celebrates someone lost being found. Neither the younger son's proposed job nor the older son's years of service explain the feast as a payment of wages.

originalReading.text: The father explains the reunion and goes out to invite the resentful brother. Luke leaves the brother’s response unstated. The listener is left with a doorway, not a report that everyone has already reconciled.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The father invites the older brother to the reunion, but Luke does not say whether he enters. The ending leaves his response open rather than reporting that everyone reconciled.

originalReading.text: The Samaritan acts as a neighbor across a boundary; the older brother stands outside his own family’s feast. Comparing the two stories makes “inside” and “outside” less comfortable labels. This is our comparison, not a claim that the stories are identical.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The Samaritan helps across a religious boundary, while the older brother stays outside his own family's feast. Being an expected insider does not necessarily mean acting as a neighbour or joining the welcome.

originalReading.text: In Exodus 16, the Israelites receive manna in the wilderness. They describe it as the bread the Lord has given them to eat. In John’s later discussion, the crowd brings up this earlier story.
originalReading.attribution: Original paraphrase of Exodus 16 and John 6:30–31.

entries.newText: In Exodus, the Israelites receive manna as food in the wilderness. The crowd in John's later story brings up this earlier account of bread from heaven.

originalReading.text: The Samaritan’s compassion leads him to help a traveler; Mark’s Jesus responds to a crowd described as shepherdless. This comparison points to a shared movement toward people, not proof that Mark copied Luke’s story.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The Samaritan's compassion leads to practical care for a traveller. In Mark, Jesus's compassion leads to teaching and feeding the crowd. Both stories connect compassion with a response to people's needs.

originalReading.text: The festival notice makes Israel’s story part of the setting. This is more specific than saying that all religious meals mean the same thing.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: John places the feeding near Passover, connecting it with Israel's memory of liberation from slavery in Egypt.

originalReading.text: Both Gospels report an extraordinary feeding; Mark highlights compassion and shepherd imagery, while John develops Passover and bread-from-heaven themes. Catholic teaching treats the Gospels as testimony about Jesus, not merely as symbols. Comparing their literary emphases neither verifies the miracle by experiment nor requires dismissing their historical testimony.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial comparison of Mark 6 and John 6; Catholic framing from Dei Verbum §§12, 19.

entries.newText: Both Gospels report an extraordinary feeding. Mark places it after compassion and teaching, using the image of a shepherd. John connects it with Passover and the discussion of bread from heaven, developing his account of who Jesus is.

originalReading.text: In thesis 43 of the Ninety-five Theses, Luther says that giving to a person in poverty or lending to someone in need is better than buying an indulgence. An indulgence concerned relief from penalties associated with sin, not permission to commit a new sin. This passage values a practical act of help.
originalReading.attribution: Original paraphrase of Luther, Ninety-five Theses 43–45. Historical context is limited to this dispute, not his entire theology.

entries.newText: In 1517, Luther says that giving to a poor person or lending to someone in need is better than buying an indulgence. An indulgence concerned penalties associated with sin, not permission to commit a new sin. His statement gives practical help real value.

originalReading.text: This is an invented modern exhibition draft, not a quotation from Luther. Before printing it, check whether the supplied passage actually supports it. A single passage may challenge a sweeping headline without settling all of Luther’s theology.
originalReading.attribution: Fictional draft caption. It is deliberately provisional, not historical evidence.

entries.newText: The exhibition draft claims that Luther thinks good works do not matter. His own statement praises practical help for people in need. Check whether the headline fairly represents what he says.
Blank paper for checking the passage before printing it for the exhibit.
The four completed panels compare the roadside story, the family feast, the feeding accounts and Luther's statement about practical help.

originalReading.text: The thesis explicitly calls helping people in need a better deed. It cannot support the blanket claim that good works do not matter. This does not by itself explain how Luther relates works, faith, and justification.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: Luther calls helping people in need a better deed. That contradicts the draft's blanket claim that good works do not matter, without settling all his views on faith and salvation.

originalReading.text: The roadside reading makes practical care recognizable, and thesis 43 explicitly commends it. The exhibit can report that narrower claim. This is a comparison across texts, not proof that this particular Gospel passage caused Luther to write the thesis.
originalReading.attribution: Editorial interpretation of the paired passages; not a test of personal belief.

entries.newText: The exhibit can say that Luther commends practical help. Comparing this with the roadside story does not prove that this particular Gospel passage caused his statement.

mars.note: Dust reduces sunlight and adheres to equipment; Mars winds are not Earth-hurricane force at the same speed.

mars.title: Ingenuity mission
mars.note: Thin atmosphere demands purpose-built flight hardware; recovered scout modules are fictional mission equipment.

mars.title: NASA thermal testing
mars.note: Controlled thermal testing of spacecraft and subsystems grounds the test-chamber setting; this fictional field comparison is not a qualification procedure. The v4 matched 20-minute example readings (20→8°C bare; 20→16°C wrapped) are invented for comparison, not taken from NASA or a qualification report.

mars.title: JPL rover navigation
mars.note: Terrain assessment and route selection matter for mobility. The field ground-probe interpretation remains a simplified fictional crewed-mission technique.

mars.title: USGS: Large wind ripples on Mars
mars.note: Mars wind ripples can resemble water-worked ripples; shape alone is not sufficient evidence of water.

mars.title: JPL: Martian Streambed Evidence Rock
mars.note: Size and rounded form of embedded gravel support ancient stream interpretation. Fictional field synthesis compresses expert interpretation.

mars.title: USGS: Eolian erasure of Mars rover tracks
mars.note: Wind alters rover tracks. Our depot navigation uses permanent engineering markers, not an asserted safe route inferred from dark marks.

mars.title: NASA: Dust Devil Dance
mars.note: Dust devil tracks can loop and overprint one another. Weather correlation does not uniquely diagnose each fictional track.

mars.title: NASA: Growing Plants in Space
mars.note: Engineered growing systems and crew well-being ground gardening. Nursery optics, compatible fittings and crewed Mars logistics are fictional abstractions.

mars.title: Grundfos: starting a drained pump after standing still
mars.note: Supports the limited idea that a drained pump may need filling before use. The closed Mars process-loop fittings and compatible stored water are fictional; this is not a commissioning procedure.

atlas.title: Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), IV, pp.90–91 and 95–96: imaginary wolf/prey example and accumulation over time

The courtyard, coordinates and numerical comparisons are invented teaching reconstruction, not Alberti’s recorded experiment.

atlas.title: Leon Battista Alberti, On Painting, Book II: veil and changed viewpoint
atlas.note: Primary text in John R. Spencer’s translation (Yale University Press, 1970; first printed 1956), pp.67–68. The veil passage links a stable view with the position and distance of its centre. The authored shifted-eye alignment is a geometric application, not a quoted historical trial.

USGS: Plate-tectonic map explanation
Alfred Wegener Institute: Seafloor spreading
Caltech: Getting the Lead Out
NHGRI: Mendelian Inheritance
Epicurus, Letter to Herodotus §§63–66, primary text excerpt
Aristotle, Politics III.1, III.6–9
atlas.note: Primary text, Jowett translation. Citizenship, common advantage and constitutional distinctions; not modern universal citizenship.

atlas.title: Plato, Republic VI, ship analogy (488a–489a)
atlas.note: Primary text. The skilled navigator is an argument about knowledge and rule, not an empirical proof of philosopher government.

atlas.title: Justinian, Institutes I.2–5 and proem
atlas.note: Primary text, Moyle translation. Natural freedom, slavery, manumission and legal statuses belong to one sixth-century legal compilation.

atlas.title: UC Berkeley, The Medieval Law School: manuscripts of Justinian with glosses
atlas.note: Collection evidence for Bologna study, marginal interpretation and later circulation of the sixth-century compilation.

atlas.title: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan XVII–XVIII and XXI (1651)
atlas.note: Primary text. Authorization is a covenant among subjects, not a contract signed by the sovereign; the sovereign may be a person or assembly.

atlas.title: John Locke, Second Treatise §§95–99, 119–122, 221–222 (1689/90)
atlas.note: Primary text. Consent, majority action, tacit consent and breach of trust are disputed arguments, not a history in which everybody actually consented.

atlas.title: Constitution of Saint-Domingue, 1801, arts.1–5, 14–16, 28
atlas.note: Primary document in translation. Abolition, French sovereignty, compulsory agricultural continuity and life governorship coexist.

atlas.title: Library of Congress / Bibliothèque Haïtienne des Pères du Saint-Esprit: Laws of Saint-Domingue (1801)
atlas.note: Primary printed law collection and archival catalogue; agency and institutions are not reduced to European pamphlets.

atlas.title: Haitian Declaration of Independence (1804), Dubois/Garrigus translation
atlas.note: Primary declaration; permanent separation from France is not a promise of equal power or an end to coercive labour.

atlas.title: BnF, Haiti’s independence debt: archival context, 1794–1922
atlas.note: Institutional historical account. Independence in 1804; recognition and coercive indemnity came later, not automatic equal standing.

atlas.title: Mémorial de l’abolition de l’esclavage, chronology of abolition
atlas.note: Institutional chronology: 1791 uprising, local abolition in 1793, national extension in February 1794. Precise local sequences were not collapsed to one decree.

atlas.title: Einstein, Relativity: The Special and General Theory, §§8–9
atlas.note: Primary teaching thought experiment. Reception order alone does not establish relative simultaneity; equal midpoint distances and invariant light speed remain required.

atlas.title: USGS: How are different map projections used?
atlas.note: Authoritative support for navigation-oriented projections and Mercator high-latitude area distortion. This reference supports cartographic properties, not a claimed historical transmission from Renaissance painting.

atlas.title: NGA Office of Geomatics: Coordinate Systems, grids and geographic references
atlas.note: Authoritative explanation of locating places by latitude and longitude. Supports the geographic reference concept, not the date or origin of historical coordinate systems.

elements.title: Corning Museum of Glass: frequently asked questions
elements.note: Soda-lime glass has more ingredients than sand and heat; abstraction explicitly disclosed.

elements.title: Kew: A brief history of plants in books
CPSC: Soap business guidance
elements.note: Supports fats/oils and alkali relationship only. No procedure implied.

elements.title: Science Museum Group: Model of a pendulum clock based on Galileo’s design
Domokos et al., How River Rocks Round: Resolving the Shape-Size Paradox
elements.note: Primary experimental research supports abrasion/rounding during transport, not instantaneous shaping by water.

elements.title: Hackney Museum: Hammerstone
elements.note: Museum describes hand-held cobbles used for striking, supporting a blunt tool distinct from an edged axe.

elements.title: V&A: Richard Batterham — methods of making
elements.note: Supports forming clay vessels on a rotating wheel and distinguishes forming from later firing. Does not establish that a bare cart wheel is a complete pottery tool.

elements.title: V&A: Lucie Rie — a Modernist revolution in British studio ceramics
elements.note: Documents clay and glaze brought to vitrifying temperature, including single firing. Supports the distinction between coating, firing and glassy surface; not a game recipe manufacturing procedure.

elements.title: Prehistoric metal mining in Britain: the study of cobble stone mining tools based on artefact study, ethnography and experimentation
elements.note: Archaeological evidence for stone percussion tools in mining. The game uses an exposed-seam pounding action rather than implying pickaxe tunnelling.

elements.title: V&A: What is tapestry?
elements.note: Explains coloured weft threads woven through warp held on a loom to create a pattern. Supports using thread rather than finished cloth as the weaving input.

elements.title: Auckland Museum: For the Want of a Nail
elements.note: Museum account of reheating iron and nailmaking with smithing/heading tools. Supports explicit hot-working context, not an extra hot-iron inventory chore.

elements.title: FAO: Principles of oil extraction
elements.note: Distinguishes crushing from expression; the authored press supplies pressure and drainage, without an industrial refining chain.

elements.title: Met Office: Make your own rain gauge
elements.note: Supports a transparent vessel with a visible external scale. This candidate deliberately claims only relative fill levels, not calibrated rainfall depth.

kitchen.title: OpenStax: What Our Ancestors Knew
kitchen.note: Fermentation history; not exact recipe ratios or a universal chronology.

kitchen.title: Aspall: Vinegar Production
kitchen.note: Producer account of alcohol-to-acid conversion and oxygen supply; no home-preservation guarantee.

kitchen.title: John Evelyn: Acetaria (1699)
kitchen.note: Primary historical salad text; period health beliefs are not accepted science.

kitchen.title: NLM: Shakespeare and the Four Humors
kitchen.note: Discarded historical theory; no medical efficacy mechanic.

kitchen.title: A. Escoffier: A Guide to Modern Cookery
kitchen.note: Primary culinary source for sauces, pastry, puddings and desserts; not invention dates. Common game preparations are simplified, not exact reproductions.

kitchen.title: King Arthur: Pie Crust guide
kitchen.note: Fat-in-flour crumbs need water to become dough.

kitchen.title: King Arthur: Classic Puff Pastry
kitchen.note: Distinct folded butter layers; preparation is compressed.

kitchen.title: UK Parliament: Trade Routes and the Slave Trade
kitchen.note: Context for sugar trade and enslaved labour; not recipe evidence.

kitchen.title: King Arthur: Pastry Cream
kitchen.note: Egg yolks, milk, sugar and starch cooked into pastry filling; game separates pouring custard from starch-thickened cream.

kitchen.title: King Arthur: Pâte à Choux
kitchen.note: Cooked flour paste and egg enrichment; shaping and baking compressed.

kitchen.title: USDA NAL: How Did We Can?
kitchen.note: History of heat processing and sealed containers, not a safe procedure.

kitchen.title: NCHFP: Ensuring Safe Canned Foods
kitchen.note: Specific validated processes matter; game does not teach canning or certify safety.

kitchen.title: European Cocoa Association: Processing
kitchen.note: Industry association process account for nibs, paste, cocoa butter, refining and conching; not a homemade chocolate recipe.

kitchen.title: Goethe-Institut: Marzipan
kitchen.note: First-party cultural recipe explicitly blends icing sugar with finely ground almonds before adding water; proportions and kneading are compressed in the game.

kitchen.title: King Arthur Baking School: French Macaron
kitchen.note: First-party teaching recipe for almond-sugar mixture folded into meringue; exact formula is not reproduced.

kitchen.title: Giada De Laurentiis: Roasted Root Vegetable Salad
kitchen.note: Pairing support only, not an exact reproduction.

kitchen.title: Colman’s Mustard: Foodservice
kitchen.note: Producer guidance lists mustard powder for vinaigrettes. It does not specify this game’s exact quantity or mixing order.

kitchen.title: Richard Ligon: A True & Exact History of the Island of Barbados (1657), pp. 22–23, 113–116
kitchen.note: Primary colonial account, consulted directly. Supports this optional, geographically and temporally bounded game-author paraphrase; not a modern recipe method or enslaved people’s own testimony.

divinity.title: Augustine, Enchiridion §§9–15, 23–27, 42–52
divinity.note: Created goodness, evil as privation, and the fallen will.

divinity.title: Augustine, On the Grace of Christ I
divinity.note: Grace as inward help for willing and acting, beyond nature and instruction alone.

divinity.title: Book of Two Principles, translated selections
divinity.note: A surviving radical-dualist argument from thirteenth-century Italy; use the translated primary text, not the page’s unqualified proposed Manichaean genealogy.

divinity.title: Occitan ritual, Lyon PA 36, Marvyn Roy Harris critical edition (Rialto)
divinity.note: Critical text IV.15–18 cites Acts 8:14–17 (not Acts 19). III.22–31 and IV.49–53 support indwelling Spirit, forgiveness and bodily enactment. Distinct witness from Two Principles.

divinity.title: Aquinas, Summa I q.1 aa.1,8
divinity.note: Reason and revelation; grace perfects nature. Augustine is an explicit authority in this question.

divinity.title: Aquinas, Summa III q.60 aa.3,6
divinity.note: Sensible signs and words; explicitly cites Augustine on the word and element.

divinity.title: Aquinas, Summa III q.62 a.1
divinity.note: God as principal cause and the sacrament as instrument; no independent magic in matter.

divinity.title: Aquinas, Summa III q.75 aa.2,4,5
divinity.note: Change of substance with sensible appearances remaining.

divinity.title: Luther, Ninety-Five Theses (1517), Taylor edition
divinity.note: Especially theses 1, 27–28, 36, 43 and 62; indulgences concern penalties, not a legitimate purchase of guilt’s forgiveness.

divinity.title: Matthew 7:18, King James Version
divinity.note: Public-domain translation supplies the visible biblical quotation; the medieval treatise’s interpretation is separately attributed.

divinity.title: Book of Two Principles I.8–10, III.1–2 and V.1–6, translated primary text
divinity.note: Online transcription based on Wakefield and Evans, with editor changes; primary text located through the search index because direct fetch failed. Use the actual argument, not the archive’s triumphalist introduction. I.9 gives the watcher analogy and I.10 its reply; V exposes disagreement among dualist groups.

divinity.title: Genesis 1:31, King James Version
divinity.note: Brief excerpt from the creation account; not an independent demonstration of the theological claim.

divinity.title: Romans 7:19, King James Version
divinity.note: Short excerpt about willing and doing. Augustine’s reading is an interpretation, not the only reading of Romans.

divinity.title: Aquinas, Summa I q.49 aa.1–3
divinity.note: Actual objections, Augustine citations, two principles, good nature and defective agency. No evidence here that Aquinas was answering this surviving Italian treatise.

divinity.title: Luther, Concerning Christian Liberty (1520), Project Gutenberg primary text
divinity.note: Public-domain English text checked for gift, faith, service and bodily discipline. The discipline discussion excludes works as righteousness before God; the bishop comparison denies their making the Christian more holy. Original paraphrases, not quotations from the separate modern Hanover translation.

divinity.title: Matthew 5:44, King James Version
divinity.note: Public-domain English enemy-love fragment. The ritual includes enemy-love and prayer/blessing for persecutors in IV.32; do not imply the manuscript used KJV.

divinity.title: Zwingli, On the Lord’s Supper (1526), Second and Third Articles
divinity.note: Primary text after THE TEXT; G. W. Bromiley, Zwingli and Bullinger (1953), pp.185–238. Original paraphrases only; the editorial introduction is not Zwingli. Ring at Third Article; ascension at Second Article. The brief supper quotation is separately attributed to KJV Luke 22:19.

divinity.title: Luther, Large Catechism V, The Sacrament of the Altar (1529)
divinity.note: Large Catechism V §§8–18 identity; §§20–29 forgiveness and nourishment of faith; §§33–37 benefit through faith. No later Formula of Concord labels substituted.

divinity.title: The Marburg Articles, 3 October 1529, Articles 1, 5–8 and 15
divinity.note: Primary joint statement, translated by Ellen Yutzy Glebe; original paraphrases only. Article 15 affirms spiritual reception, records corporal-presence disagreement, and qualifies mutual love by conscience. A signature is not doctrinal convergence.

divinity.title: Council of Trent, Session VI, Decree on Justification, 13 January 1547
divinity.note: Session VI V–VIII: prior help, consent, unearned initial gift and inward renewal; X and canon24: growth in received justice. Compare Luther’s explicit more-sacred-person exclusion, not only temporal order.

divinity.title: Calvin, Institutes I.11 §§9–13 (1559), Beveridge translation
divinity.note: Painting and sculpture, devotional honour, and instituted signs. Calvin’s polemical historical allegations are not independent findings. Especially §§12–13.

divinity.title: Calvin, Treatise on Relics (1543), Krasinski translation, second edition 1870
divinity.note: Calvin begins at printed p.217; the preceding dissertation and numbered translator notes are not his text. Catalogue pp.254–256; admission concerning commissioners pp.276–277; genuine-or-false distinction p.278. Reports are attributed, not authenticated.

divinity.title: Council of Trent, Session XXV (3–4 December 1563), Waterworth 1848, pp.233–236
divinity.note: Decree on invocation, relics and images. Distinguish image-honour, holy bodies, new-relic recognition and episcopal approval of unusual images. The fictional case receives no invented real ruling.

divinity.title: Augustine, On the Trinity V.1,5–9
divinity.note: Primary text, public-domain translation. Relative names, one divine being, and limits of creaturely comparison.

divinity.title: Aquinas, Summa I q.28 aa.1–3
divinity.note: Relations and divine unity. Explicitly reopens Augustine; not three members of a species.

divinity.title: Aquinas, Summa I q.32 a.1
divinity.note: Natural reason does not demonstrate the Trinity; an explanation of a received belief is not its proof.

divinity.title: Calvin, Institutes III.20 §§19–27
divinity.note: Primary text, Beveridge translation. Distinguishes mutual prayer among the living from invoking departed saints; challenges scriptural warrant and knowledge of particular prayers.

divinity.title: John 17:1, King James Version
divinity.note: Brief public-domain quotation. Its Trinitarian interpretation is separately attributed.

divinity.title: Luke 22:19, King James Version
divinity.note: Brief public-domain quotation; rival readings do not become the words of the verse.

light.title: USCCB — Doctrinal Elements of a Curriculum Framework
light.note: Current resource page links the 2011 file of the framework first printed in 2008. Supporting scope reference, not a full-course checklist.

light.title: Luke 10 — World English Bible Classic
light.note: Luke 10:25–37; very brief exact quotations and original paraphrase.

light.title: World English Bible — Public-domain statement
light.note: Only exact brief Gospel quotations are labeled as WEB text; paraphrases are clearly labeled.

light.title: Vatican II — Dei Verbum
light.note: §§12, 18–19: literary form and Gospel witness; Catholic framing.

light.title: UNESCO — Jikji
light.note: Earlier East Asian movable-metal-type printing; chronology safeguard.

light.title: National Library of Scotland — Martin Luther and the Reformation
light.note: Print circulation and surviving pamphlets; do not adopt the page’s simplified indulgence analogy.

light.title: Luther — Ninety-five Theses
light.note: Primary theses, especially 43–45; no nailing-to-door claim.

light.title: Leviticus 19 — World English Bible Classic
light.note: 19:34, love of the stranger; public-domain translation.
